description.value: An fMRI study testing whether self-expanding cooperative games attenuate cigarette-cue reactivity among nicotine-deprived smokers.

spans.text: We tested this model among nicotine-deprived smokers who, during fMRI scanning, played a series of two-player cooperative games with a relationship partner.

value: We predicted that the self-expansion reward of participating in a socially-shared novel, challenging, and exciting activity would undermine nicotine craving and result in less activation in cigarette-cue related brain areas such as the ventral striatum, temporo-parietal junction (TPJ), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and amygdala [27].

spans.text: In the current study, couples in long-term relationships played cooperative games together that were either self-expanding (particularly exciting, novel, and challenging) or not, and in which a cigarette cue did or did not appear.

responded with their dominant hand using a four-button response box

instructions.value: Couples played cooperative two-player games. Each player marked the position of a feather target among four horizontally presented images by pressing the corresponding button or keyboard key. Players earned points for correct selections, received visible feedback, and received a team-score deduction for incorrect selections.

spans.text: The goal of the two-player game was for each member of the couple to “mark” when a feather (the target) was presented by pressing buttons on the button-box (or keyboard) that corresponded to the positions of the feather.

stimuli.value: Four simultaneous black-and-white images of everyday objects, including feather targets and, in cigarette-cue blocks, an image of a lit cigarette. Self-expanding blocks used novel images, whereas non-self-expanding blocks used images seen during practice.

spans.text: Each block consisted of a series of trials where 4 black-and-white images simultaneously appeared horizontally on the screen

value: Post-block ratings of cigarette craving, game pleasantness, game excitement, positive mood, and negative mood on 1-to-4 scales

spans.text: Following each game block, participants responded to five questions on a 1 (“not at all”) to 4 (“extremely”) scale
